questions.stem: Which Vaughan Williams class primarily blocks fast sodium channels?
questions.explanation: Class I antiarrhythmics are sodium-channel blockers that slow conduction in fast-response tissue.

questions.stem: Which class prolongs repolarization mainly by blocking potassium channels?
questions.explanation: Class III drugs block potassium channels, prolonging repolarization and refractory period.

questions.stem: A stable patient has a regular narrow-complex SVT dependent on the AV node. Which drug is the lecture's rapid AV-node 'off switch'?
questions.explanation: Adenosine briefly blocks AV nodal conduction and is used for AV-node-dependent re-entrant SVT.

questions.stem: Why must adenosine be given as a rapid IV bolus?

options.A: It has a half-life of about 10 seconds
options.C: It is poorly absorbed from muscle

questions.explanation: Adenosine has an extremely short half-life of about 10 seconds, so rapid IV administration is required.

questions.stem: Which condition is a major contraindication to adenosine in this lecture?
questions.explanation: Adenosine may cause bronchospasm and is contraindicated in asthma.

questions.stem: A patient has an irregularly irregular narrow-complex tachycardia with no consistent P waves. Which strategy is appropriate for ventricular rate control?

options.A: Beta blocker or non-DHP calcium-channel blocker

questions.explanation: For atrial fibrillation, the lecture uses beta blockers or non-DHP calcium-channel blockers to slow AV nodal conduction for rate control.

questions.stem: A wide, regular tachycardia should be considered which rhythm until proven otherwise?
questions.explanation: The lecture emphasizes that a wide-complex tachycardia should be treated as ventricular tachycardia until proven otherwise.

questions.stem: A patient with tachyarrhythmia is hypotensive and confused but still has a pulse. What is the immediate treatment?
questions.explanation: Hemodynamic instability with tachyarrhythmia and a pulse requires synchronized cardioversion before detailed drug selection.

questions.stem: Which drug is specifically highlighted for torsades de pointes?
questions.explanation: Magnesium suppresses early afterdepolarizations and is used for torsades de pointes.

questions.stem: Which class reduces sympathetic effects, automaticity, and AV nodal conduction?
questions.explanation: Class II beta blockers reduce sympathetic cardiac effects, decreasing automaticity and AV nodal conduction.

questions.stem: Verapamil and diltiazem belong to which Vaughan Williams class?
questions.explanation: Non-dihydropyridine calcium-channel blockers are Class IV antiarrhythmics and slow AV nodal conduction.

questions.stem: Which Class I subgroup causes moderate sodium-channel block and increases action-potential duration?
questions.explanation: Class IA has moderate sodium-channel block and also prolongs action-potential duration.

questions.stem: Which adverse effect is especially associated with procainamide in the lecture?
questions.explanation: Procainamide can cause a lupus-like syndrome, especially in slow acetylators.

questions.stem: A patient has very fast irregular wide-complex AF with WPW. Which AV-nodal blocker should be avoided?

options.D: None; AV nodal blockade is preferred

questions.explanation: In pre-excited AF, AV-nodal blockers such as adenosine can favor rapid accessory-pathway conduction and should be avoided.

questions.stem: What is the key electrophysiologic effect of Class IC drugs such as flecainide?

options.A: Strong slowing of conduction with little effect on AP duration
options.B: Marked shortening of AV nodal refractory period

questions.explanation: Class IC drugs strongly block sodium channels and markedly slow conduction with little effect on action-potential duration.

questions.stem: Which cardiac property cannot be directly assessed from a surface ECG?
questions.explanation: The lecture states that ECG evaluates electrical properties but not force of contraction or ejection fraction.

questions.stem: A depolarization wave moving toward the positive exploring electrode produces:
questions.explanation: Depolarization moving toward the positive electrode gives a positive/upward ECG deflection.

questions.stem: A repolarization wave moving away from the positive electrode produces:
questions.explanation: For repolarization, movement away from the positive electrode produces a positive/upward deflection.

questions.stem: The P wave represents:
questions.explanation: The P wave represents atrial depolarization.

questions.stem: The QRS complex represents:
questions.explanation: QRS is ventricular depolarization; atrial repolarization is usually hidden within it.

questions.stem: Why is atrial repolarization usually not visible on the ECG?

options.A: It occurs with ventricular depolarization and is masked by the larger QRS
options.D: It is identical to the T wave

questions.explanation: Atrial repolarization overlaps ventricular depolarization and is obscured by the larger QRS complex.

questions.stem: A PR interval longer than 0.20 s most directly suggests:
questions.explanation: The normal PR interval is about 0.12–0.20 s; prolongation indicates conduction delay/block.

questions.stem: A QRS duration of 0.16 s suggests:
questions.explanation: Normal QRS is under 0.12 s; widening suggests delayed ventricular conduction such as bundle branch block.

questions.stem: Which ECG interval includes both ventricular depolarization and repolarization?
questions.explanation: The QT interval spans ventricular depolarization through repolarization.

questions.stem: A prolonged QT interval increases the risk of:
questions.explanation: The lecture links prolonged QT to ventricular arrhythmias, particularly torsades de pointes.

questions.stem: At 25 mm/s, how many large ECG squares equal one second?
questions.explanation: At standard speed, five large horizontal squares equal one second.

questions.stem: A regular rhythm has 4 large squares between consecutive R waves. The approximate heart rate is:
questions.explanation: For regular rhythm, rate ≈ 300 divided by large squares between R waves: 300/4 = 75/min.

questions.stem: Which finding is required for normal sinus rhythm in this lecture?

options.A: Each P wave is followed by a QRS and each QRS is preceded by a P wave

questions.explanation: Normal sinus rhythm is regular, 60–100/min, with a P before every QRS and normal PR/QRS durations.

questions.stem: Which leads are used in the lecture's quick approach to estimating the electrical axis?
questions.explanation: Lead I and aVF view the heart near 0° and +90° and are used to estimate axis.

questions.stem: The normal electrical axis range given in the lecture is approximately:
questions.explanation: The lecture gives a normal axis from about −30° to +90°.

questions.stem: In healthy vessels, endothelial hemostatic balance is normally shifted toward:
questions.explanation: Healthy endothelium favors anticoagulant and profibrinolytic activity.

questions.stem: Which endothelial mediators both inhibit platelet aggregation and promote vasodilation?
questions.explanation: Nitric oxide and prostacyclin inhibit platelet aggregation and dilate vessels.

questions.stem: Thrombomodulin limits coagulation mainly by inhibiting which activated factors in this lecture?
questions.explanation: The lecture lists thrombomodulin as inhibiting factors Va and VIIIa.

questions.stem: Heparan sulfate on healthy endothelium enhances the activity of:
questions.explanation: Heparan sulfate enhances antithrombin III, which inhibits thrombin and factor Xa.

questions.stem: Which endothelial product promotes fibrinolysis?
questions.explanation: tPA activates plasmin and promotes fibrin clot breakdown.

questions.stem: Damaged endothelium promotes platelet adhesion mainly by releasing:
questions.explanation: vWF promotes platelet adhesion to exposed collagen after endothelial injury.

questions.stem: Which mediator is a potent endothelial-derived vasoconstrictor?
questions.explanation: Endothelin-1 is a potent vasoconstrictor that stimulates vascular smooth-muscle contraction.

questions.stem: Which capillary type has the greatest permeability?
questions.explanation: Sinusoidal/discontinuous capillaries, such as in liver, have very high permeability.

questions.stem: A patient with long-standing diabetes develops endothelial dysfunction. Which change is expected?

options.B: Increased NO and decreased adhesion molecules

questions.explanation: Chronic endothelial dysfunction shifts toward vasoconstriction and inflammation with lower NO and higher endothelin-1.

questions.stem: Why does increased endothelial permeability promote atherosclerosis?

options.A: It allows LDL to enter the vessel wall and contributes to foam-cell/plaque formation

questions.explanation: The lecture links increased permeability to LDL entry into the wall, foam-cell formation, and plaque development.

questions.stem: Which adhesion molecules are increased in chronic endothelial activation?
questions.explanation: Activated endothelium increases VCAM-1 and ICAM-1 to recruit immune cells.

questions.stem: Which factor is listed as a cause of endothelial dysfunction?
questions.explanation: Smoking is one of several listed contributors to endothelial dysfunction.

questions.stem: Endothelial VEGF production is most directly related to:
questions.explanation: VEGF promotes formation of new blood vessels as part of endothelial angiogenic function.

questions.stem: During acute endothelial dysfunction, histamine and bradykinin contribute to swelling mainly by causing:
questions.explanation: Acute inflammatory mediators increase vascular permeability, allowing plasma leakage and swelling.

questions.stem: Statins are listed as a strategy for endothelial dysfunction because they:

options.A: Reduce atherosclerosis progression and improve endothelial function

questions.explanation: The lecture lists lipid-lowering therapy with statins as a strategy to improve endothelial function and reduce atherosclerosis progression.

questions.stem: Which event marks the beginning of ventricular systole?
questions.explanation: Isovolumetric contraction begins ventricular systole.

questions.stem: During isovolumetric contraction, ventricular volume remains constant because:
questions.explanation: All valves are closed, so pressure rises without filling or ejection.

questions.stem: The aortic valve opens when:

options.B: Left ventricular pressure exceeds aortic pressure
options.D: Ventricular pressure falls below atrial pressure

questions.explanation: Ejection begins when ventricular pressure rises above aortic pressure.

questions.stem: Approximately what fraction of ventricular ejection occurs during rapid ejection in this lecture?
questions.explanation: The lecture states that about 70% of ejected blood leaves during rapid ejection.

questions.stem: The second heart sound is caused by closure of the:
questions.explanation: S2 occurs with closure of the aortic and pulmonary valves at the start of ventricular diastole.

questions.stem: During isovolumetric relaxation, which combination is correct?
questions.explanation: The ventricles relax while all valves are closed, so pressure falls at constant volume.

questions.stem: AV valves open when ventricular pressure:
questions.explanation: Atrial pressure exceeding ventricular pressure creates the gradient that opens the AV valves.

questions.stem: During ventricular filling, volume changes from:
questions.explanation: Filling increases ventricular volume from end-systolic toward end-diastolic volume.

questions.stem: Atrial systole contributes approximately:
questions.explanation: Atrial contraction contributes about 20–25% of ventricular filling.

questions.stem: A third heart sound is associated with:
questions.explanation: S3 occurs with rapid inflow into the ventricle and is normally more likely in children.

questions.stem: A fourth heart sound is produced during:
questions.explanation: S4 is ventricular wall vibration during atrial contraction and is associated with a stiff ventricle.

questions.stem: At a heart rate of 75/min, cardiac-cycle duration is approximately:
questions.explanation: Cardiac cycle duration = 60/HR; 60/75 = 0.8 seconds.

questions.stem: Which phase has neither filling nor ejection?
questions.explanation: During isovolumetric contraction all valves are closed, so there is neither filling nor ejection.

questions.stem: During rapid filling, approximately what proportion of filling occurs?
questions.explanation: The lecture states that 60–70% of ventricular filling occurs during rapid filling.

questions.stem: Why does aortic pressure fall while the aortic valve is closed?

options.A: Blood continues to leave the aorta toward the periphery
options.B: The ventricle ejects into the aorta
options.C: The AV valves force blood into the aorta

questions.explanation: With no new ventricular inflow, blood continues to run off into the peripheral circulation, lowering aortic pressure.

cards.front: What does Vaughan Williams Class I block?
cards.back: Fast Na+ channels; it slows conduction in fast-response tissue.

cards.front: How do IA, IB, and IC differ?
cards.back: IA: moderate Na+ block + ↑APD; IB: weak Na+ block + ↓APD; IC: strong conduction slowing with little APD change.
Beta blockade → ↓sympathetic effects, ↓automaticity, and ↓AV nodal conduction.

cards.front: Why is adenosine given rapidly IV?
cards.back: Its half-life is about 10 seconds.

cards.front: Major adenosine contraindications in this lecture?
cards.back: AV block and asthma; bronchospasm can occur.

cards.front: What is the first question in tachyarrhythmia?
cards.back: Is the patient hemodynamically stable or unstable?

cards.front: Unstable tachyarrhythmia with a pulse: treatment?
cards.back: Synchronized cardioversion.

cards.front: Wide-complex tachycardia should be considered what until proven otherwise?
cards.back: Ventricular tachycardia.

cards.front: Drug highlighted for torsades de pointes?
cards.back: Magnesium sulfate.

cards.front: Why avoid AV-nodal blockers in pre-excited AF/WPW?
cards.back: The AV node acts as a brake; blocking it can favor rapid accessory-pathway conduction.
QT prolongation/torsades, hypotension, negative inotropy, and SLE-like syndrome.

cards.front: Rate control options for AF emphasized in the lecture?
cards.back: Beta blocker or non-DHP calcium-channel blocker in an appropriate patient.

cards.front: What does a surface ECG record?
cards.back: The summed electrical activity of many myocardial cells, not a single action potential.

cards.front: Which cardiac property cannot ECG directly assess?
cards.back: Contractility/force of contraction or ejection fraction.

cards.front: Depolarization moving toward a positive electrode gives what deflection?
cards.back: Positive/upward.

cards.front: Repolarization moving away from a positive electrode gives what deflection?
cards.back: Positive/upward.

cards.front: What does the QT interval represent?
cards.back: Ventricular depolarization plus repolarization.
It increases risk of ventricular arrhythmias, especially torsades de pointes.

cards.front: At 25 mm/s, how much time is 5 large squares?
cards.back: 1 second.

cards.front: Quick leads for axis estimation and normal range?
cards.back: Use I and aVF; normal axis is about −30° to +90°.

cards.front: Healthy endothelium favors thrombosis or antithrombosis?
cards.back: Antithrombosis: anticoagulant and profibrinolytic activity predominates.
Vasodilation and inhibition of platelet aggregation.
Inhibits activated factors Va and VIIIa in this lecture.
Enhances antithrombin III → inhibits thrombin and factor Xa.
tPA promotes fibrinolysis via plasmin; PAI-1 inhibits fibrinolysis.

cards.front: What does damaged endothelium release to promote platelet adhesion?
cards.back: von Willebrand factor (vWF).
Endothelin-1.
Continuous < fenestrated < discontinuous/sinusoidal.
It controls leukocyte adhesion/migration using molecules such as selectins, ICAMs, and VCAM-1.
Produces growth factors such as VEGF to promote new-vessel formation.

cards.front: Chronic endothelial dysfunction: NO and endothelin-1 changes?
cards.back: ↓NO and ↑endothelin-1.

cards.front: How does endothelial dysfunction promote atherosclerosis?
cards.back: ↑permeability lets LDL enter the wall; inflammation and adhesion recruit cells, promoting foam cells/plaque.
Hyperglycemia, insulin resistance, dyslipidemia, obesity, hypertension, smoking, inactivity, inflammation, oxidative stress, and aging.

cards.front: Acute inflammatory endothelial dysfunction causes edema how?
cards.back: Inflammatory mediators increase vascular permeability, allowing plasma leakage.

cards.front: Therapeutic approaches listed for endothelial dysfunction?
cards.back: Improve NO, reduce oxidative stress/inflammation, lipid lowering (statins), EPC therapy, and targeted endothelial signaling.

cards.front: Main phases of the cardiac cycle?
cards.back: Atrial systole → isovolumetric contraction → ejection → isovolumetric relaxation → filling.

cards.front: Atrial systole contributes how much ventricular filling?
cards.back: About 20–25%.
Ventricular wall vibration during atrial contraction; associated with a stiff ventricle.
All valves closed; ventricular pressure rises; volume stays constant.
Closure of AV valves at the start of ventricular systole/isovolumetric contraction.
Ventricular pressure rising above aortic/pulmonary arterial pressure.
About 70% of ejection occurs rapidly, then about 30% during reduced ejection.
All valves closed; ventricular pressure falls; volume remains constant.
Closure of the semilunar valves at the beginning of ventricular diastole.
Ventricular pressure falling below atrial pressure.

cards.front: How much filling occurs during rapid filling?
cards.back: About 60–70%.
Rapid inflow into the ventricles during rapid filling; it may be normal in children.

cards.front: Why does aortic pressure fall while the aortic valve is closed?
cards.back: Blood continues to run off from the aorta into the peripheral circulation while no new ventricular blood enters.
